label: Chapter 5: Napoleon, Waterloo and the Revolution of 1830

units.text: The French years were short, but they changed Brussels more than almost any other period.
After the annexation of 1795, the revolutionary government set about erasing the old order.
Monasteries and convents were closed, and their lands and buildings were sold off.
Many medieval churches and abbeys, some of them centuries old, were demolished or turned into barracks, warehouses, and factories.
The guilds were abolished. Feudal privileges disappeared.
In their place, France introduced new laws, new weights and measures, and eventually the Napoleonic Code, which became the basis of Belgian civil law.
For ordinary people, the most unpopular novelty was conscription.
Young men from Brussels and its countryside were drafted into Napoleon's armies, and many never came back.
Napoleon himself visited Brussels more than once, and he used the royal estate at Laeken, on the northern edge of the city, as a residence.
It would later become the home of the Belgian royal family.
Even after his fall, the artist who had painted his coronation, Jacques-Louis David, chose Brussels as his place of exile.
He lived there from 1816 until he died in 1825.
The end of the empire came with startling closeness to Brussels.
In 1814, Napoleon was defeated and exiled, and the Congress of Vienna, as we heard in the story of Luxembourg, redrew the map.

The great powers decided that France's northern neighbors needed to be stronger, so they combined the old Austrian Netherlands with the Dutch Republic to create a single United Kingdom of the Netherlands, under King William the First.
The new kingdom had two capitals.
Government and parliament met alternately in The Hague and in Brussels.
Then, in March of 1815, Napoleon escaped from the island of Elba and returned to France.
For about a hundred days, he ruled again, and he marched north to strike the allied armies that were gathering in Belgium, under the Duke of Wellington and the Prussian Field Marshal Blücher.
Brussels, in June 1815, was filled with British and allied officers and their families.
On the evening of the fifteenth of June, the Duchess of Richmond held a famous ball in the city for Wellington and his officers.
In the middle of the evening, news arrived that Napoleon's army had crossed the border and was advancing.
Officers slipped out of the ball, still in their dress uniforms, and marched south to fight.
The scene became so famous that the poet Lord Byron, who visited Brussels a year later, wrote some of his best-known verses about that night of dancing and the sound of guns.
Three days later, on the eighteenth of June, the decisive battle was fought at a village about fifteen kilometers south of Brussels.
It was called Waterloo. On that field, the Allied armies, with Wellington's British, Dutch, and Belgian troops and Blücher's Prussians, crushed Napoleon's army and ended his career for good.
In Brussels, people could hear the cannon, and in the days that followed the city was filled with thousands of wounded soldiers, who were treated in houses, churches, and makeshift hospitals.
With Napoleon gone, the new Kingdom of the Netherlands got to work.
King William was a hardworking, practical ruler who promoted industry, canals, schools, and a modern economy.
Brussels flourished. The city got a new opera house, the Théâtre de la Monnaie, which opened in 1819, on the site of the old royal mint.
But the kingdom had a basic flaw.
The north was mostly Protestant and Dutch-speaking, and the south was mostly Catholic, with a French-speaking upper class and a Dutch-speaking, Flemish population.
The king favored the Dutch language and the north in appointments and taxation.
French-speaking liberals resented his controls over the press and the schools, and Catholics resented his interference in the church.
In 1828, these two groups, who normally disliked each other, joined forces against the king.
It was the beginning of the end.
And then came the night at the opera.
On the twenty-fifth of August, 1830, there was a performance at the Monnaie of a popular French opera called The Mute Girl of Portici.
It told the story of a revolt in seventeenth-century Naples against Spanish rule, and it contained a stirring duet about love of country.
As the singers reached that number, the audience was swept up.
They poured out of the theater into the streets, shouting, and joined crowds that were already angry about food prices and unemployment.
Over the next days, mobs attacked the houses of unpopular officials and the offices of a pro-government newspaper.
Similar riots broke out in other towns.
At first it was a protest, and its leaders wanted autonomy, not independence.
But King William hesitated, then sent troops under his son, Prince Frederick, to restore order.
On the twenty-third of September, some ten thousand Dutch soldiers entered Brussels through the gates on the upper side of the city and tried to push down the hill toward the old center.
They were met by a ragged force of volunteers: workers, students, craftsmen, and men from other towns, including Liège, who had come to help.

For four days, from the twenty-third to the twenty-sixth of September, fighting raged around the Royal Park, in the streets, from house to house, over barricades made of paving stones, carts, and furniture.
By the end of the fourth night, the Dutch had pulled back.
A provisional government had already taken control in Brussels, and on the fourth of October, it declared Belgium independent.

A National Congress was elected, and in February of 1831 it adopted a constitution that was among the most liberal in Europe, with guarantees of freedom of the press, of religion, and of association, and a king with limited powers.
The Congress chose Brussels as the capital, and it sought a king acceptable to the great powers.
After much negotiation, they picked a German prince, Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, a widower of the British royal family and an uncle to the future Queen Victoria.
On the twenty-first of July, 1831, Leopold stood on the steps of a church on the Place Royale and swore an oath to the constitution.
That day, July twenty-first, is still Belgium's National Day.
The new country had to defend itself at once.
A few weeks later, in August of 1831, the Dutch army invaded in what is called the Ten Days' Campaign, and a French army had to march in to save Belgium.
It took years of negotiation before the Dutch would accept the loss.
In 1839, a treaty signed in London finally confirmed Belgium's independence, and it guaranteed the new country's perpetual neutrality, under the protection of the great powers.
The same treaty, as we heard in the story of Luxembourg, split the old duchy of Luxembourg in two, and handed its western half, including the town of Bastogne, to Belgium.
If you are walking in the center of Brussels, there are two places worth a stop.
At the Place des Martyrs, a quiet neoclassical square near the city center, a monument and a crypt honor the fighters who died in the September days of 1830.
And at the Parc de Bruxelles, the same park where the Dutch troops fought their way in and lost, you can walk among the trees and statues where the battle for Belgian independence was won.
In the next chapter, the capital of a new kingdom grows into a modern metropolis, and the king who rules it from 1865 turns it into a showcase, financed in part by a colony of terrible cruelty.
